Mean bias 0 (SD 153) and not significantly different from zero; limits of agreement read as -300 to +300. This is the tolerance the source itself reports for the group mean.
Share of women whose Mifflin-St Jeor prediction lay within 10% of measured
Healthy weight 73, overweight 76, obesity 80 percent; no separate figure for the underweight group. Individual accuracy, not a bound on the group mean.
Share of adults whose Mifflin-St Jeor prediction lay within 10% of measured
337 ambulatory community-living adults, indirect calorimetry; 87 percent in non-obese, 75 percent in obese
Abstract only; ages, sex split and mean measured rate were not on the page. Bias 95% CI -26 to +8 kcal per day (unbiased).
Share of adults whose Mifflin-St Jeor prediction differed from measured by more than 10%
130 non-hospitalised adult volunteers, BMI 18.8 to 96.8, indirect calorimetry
Abstract only; about 78 percent were within 10% by subtraction. Frankenfield 2003 (J Am Diet Assoc).
Share of adults whose Mifflin-St Jeor prediction lay within 10% of measured, handheld calorimeter
362 adults, MedGem analyzer (not a ventilated hood); Harris-Benedict 57.5, WHO/FAO/UNU 55.2 percent

Abstract only (Hasson et al. 2011); accuracy varied widely by sex, BMI, age and ethnicity, and Mifflin under-predicted in normal-weight and 40 to 60 y subgroups. Only the abstract on the record page was read.
Frankenfield 2005 systematic review, Mifflin-St Jeor within 10% of measured
Healthy non-obese and obese adults, indirect calorimetry, review of validation studies

The abstract says Mifflin-St Jeor predicted within 10% in more individuals than any other equation and had the narrowest error range, and that noteworthy errors exist for individuals; it gives no percentage.
Standing energy expenditure, adult warmblood saddle horse, from the Hanak VO2 row
12 warmblood saddle horses, mean mass 477.5 kg, VO2 4.0 (3.3 to 4.7) mL per kg per min standing in a respiratory mask (equine_resting_vo2)

Derived, not read: VO2 x 477.5 kg x 1440 min x (3.941 + 1.106 RQ) kcal per L with the Weir coefficients in oxygen_energy. RQ is not reported, so Low is VO2 3.3 at RQ 0.7 and High is VO2 4.7 at RQ 1.0; Value is VO2 4.0 at RQ 0.85. Horses were standing in a mask, not fasted or basal.
Resting oxygen consumption, healthy control horses
6 control horses (body condition score 6.4 +/- 1.2), Mazan et al. 2004, J Appl Physiol 97:91-97; RAO horses 4.93 +/- 1.30

Abstract only; value is 2.93 +/- 0.70, Low and High are mean -/+ 0.70. Body mass, RQ and the energy figure were not on the page, so kcal per day is not derived. Per kg that is about 20 to 21 kcal per kg per day with the Weir coefficients at RQ 0.7 to 1.0.
Heat production of ponies in metabolism chambers, per metabolic body mass
MJ per kg^0.75 per day (about 122 kcal per kg^0.75 per day)
Six pony geldings, open-circuit calorimetry in metabolism chambers, Fuller et al. 2004 (compared with doubly labelled water, 0.48 +/- 0.29)
Abstract only: 0.51 +/- 0.02. Low and High are mean -/+ 0.02. Fed ponies in chambers, so this is total heat production, not a resting or fasting figure; body masses were not on the page.

scurvy_consequences.title: Scurvy consequences: reopening of old wounds, gum disease and tooth loss, causes of death, and the stage or level at which each appears
scurvy_consequences.source: Lind, A Treatise of the Scurvy (1753; archive.org copy b30507054, OCR text with the long s printed as f, quoted as printed), Gandhi et al. 2023 (Diseases, PMC10296835), Pimentel 2003 (Am J Emerg Med, abstract on PubMed), Francescone and Levitt (Cutis 76(4), text as reposted by The Hospitalist), Desenclos et al. 1989 (Bull WHO, abstract) and Wikipedia's Scurvy article. Pages were read through a fetch tool that returns a summary, so quotes are as that tool returned them; Lind's chapter and stage labels are its reading of the text. Bourne 1946 (Proc Nutr Soc) opened only as scanned page images with no text, and the Deirawan 2020 pathology review (Int J Dermatol) only as an abstract, so neither contributes a row. Reference data for the Reality keeper; not a fit.
rows: Healed ulcers and old wounds break open again in scurvy
Naval and hospital cases described by Lind 1753, Chapter II (diagnostics, signs)

Lind: 'It is not unufual at this time, for fuch perfons a have had ulcers formerly healed up, to have them break out afrefh'. The fetch read the passage as belonging to the last, most severe stage. No interval, rate or share of patients is given.
Reopening of a nearly healed wound as the first sign of scurvy in one man
none found (single case; about one month from near-healed to scurvy)
John Thomas, fractured arm from a musket ball in 1742, nearly healed by November 1742, scurvy in December when fresh food was cut off (Lind, Chapter II footnote d, as the fetch summarised it)

Lind: 'The firft fymptom of which that appeared, was the breaking out of the late wounds in his arm'; he died later at Mahon hospital. The main text is read as saying weakened, immobilised parts often turn scorbutic first. One case, so it is an existence example, not a timing figure.
Mechanism the modern reviews give for failed wound repair; whether they mention old scars reopening
Gandhi et al. 2023, Diseases 11(2):78 (clinical review); Wikipedia Scurvy article

Gandhi: 'inability to finish this step of collagen synthesis has adverse effects on bone and fibroblast functions, tooth development, and wound healing'. The review does not mention healed wounds or scars reopening. Wikipedia's pathogenesis section says only that once-healed breaks (bone) may recur. The Lind 1753 and Mead 1762 reopening reports and Walter's Anson voyage account appeared only in a search summary of Bourne 1946, which did not open as text, so they are not tabled.
Time for skin lesions and other symptoms to heal after treatment starts
Adult scurvy patients given vitamin C, Gandhi et al. 2023

Gandhi: 'it can take up to 2-3 weeks for other symptoms of scurvy, such as skin lesions, to heal'. Low is 2 weeks, High is 3 weeks; the page states 'up to' 2-3 weeks, so Low is the reader's reading. No vitamin C level is given for this. Context for repair, not for loss.

Lind: 'Their gums foon after become itchy, fwelled, and are apt to bleed upon the gentleft friction'. Lind's chapter on earlier authors also notes that older writers took the putrid gums as the sure sign of the disease.
Gum findings in scurvy and what they depend on
Francescone and Levitt, Cutis 76(4); Gandhi et al. 2023

Francescone: 'gingival findings occur only in patients with teeth', listing swelling, petechial lesions, purplish discoloration, bleeding with little provocation and secondary periodontal infection. Gandhi: 'gingivitis with bleeding and receding gums, as well as dental caries', attributed to soft tissue formation and maintenance with no further mechanism given. Bleeding gums were reported in 60 percent of 30 patients in a case series (Nefihancoro 2024, via the Dismech page, unvalidated).
Weeks of inadequate vitamin C intake before the signs (including gum bleeding) appear
Gandhi et al. 2023: 'after 4 to 12 weeks of inadequate dietary ascorbic acid intake'

Low 4 weeks and High 12 weeks as days. This is the review's general onset window, not an oral-specific figure; the page gives no timing for oral signs alone. Francescone says 'weeks to months' of deficient intake (as little as 10 mg per day). Consistent with the Iowa 28-day first-sign figure in vitamin_c_depletion.
Loosening and loss of teeth in scurvy
Lind 1753, Chapter II, in the gum description after the discussion of haemorrhages (second stage by the fetch's reading); Murray's account in a footnote

Lind: 'The teeth moft commonly become quite loofe, and often fall out', followed by the remark that caries of the jaw 'does but rarely follow'. Murray's account: the already loosened teeth easily dropped out of the sockets. No timing, share of patients or vitamin C level.
Tooth loss in scurvy in modern reviews
Gandhi et al. 2023; Francescone and Levitt (Cutis); Wikipedia Scurvy article

Neither clinical review mentions tooth loss. Gandhi lists gingivitis with receding gums, dental caries, and 'tooth development' among the collagen-dependent functions. Wikipedia lists 'loosening of teeth' and, in pathogenesis, 'Teeth loosen', with no mechanism or timing. Searched; null.
Lind 1753, Chapter II (patients moved or put in fresh air) and Chapter III (exertion or a change of air)

Lind: 'They are apt, upon being moved, or expofed to the frefh air, fuddenly to expire'; 'ending in fudden, and often unexpected death'; Chapter III: 'Their dropping down dead upon an exertion of their strength, or change of air, is not easily foretold', usually after a tedious confinement in foul air. Lind also notes (of Eugalenus) that the disease 'often killed the patient before thefe fymptoms appeared'.
Cause of death in untreated scurvy, modern clinical statements
Pimentel 2003, Am J Emerg Med 21(4):328-32 (abstract); Francescone and Levitt, Cutis 76(4); Wikipedia Scurvy article

Pimentel: 'Untreated, scurvy is inevitably fatal as a result of infection or sudden death'. Francescone: 'Scurvy that is left untreated is fatal as a result of either sudden death or infection'. Wikipedia: 'death from infection or bleeding'. No case-fatality rate, time to death or vitamin C level is given. Pimentel's abstract adds that even advanced disease responds to vitamin C.
Mechanism offered for sudden death, and haemorrhage as a late feature
Gandhi et al. 2023; Francescone and Levitt (Cutis)

Gandhi: 'Dyspnea, hypotension, and sudden death have all been described as cardiorespiratory symptoms of scurvy', hypothesised to come from 'a defective vasomotor response'; no frequency or timing. Francescone: in rare extreme cases bleeding can involve the peritoneum, pericardium and adrenal glands, and the late stages are 'characterized by neuropathy, edema, oliguria, syncope, leukopenia, and intracerebral hemorrhage'.
Deaths on Anson's 1740-44 voyage, a historical mortality figure
men (of about 2000) in the first 10 months
Wikipedia Scurvy article, 18th century section ('1,300 out of 2,000' crew)

Second-hand and not all attributed to scurvy by the page. Pearce (Hektoen International, 2016) gives another framing: 'only 188 men of the original 1,854 surviving'. The two crew sizes differ, so no rate is derived. The page also says researchers estimate scurvy killed at least two million sailors in 1500-1800, attributed to unnamed researchers; not tabled as a figure.
Case-fatality rate or time to death in untreated scurvy
Gandhi 2023, Pimentel 2003 abstract, Francescone and Levitt, Desenclos 1989 abstract, two MMWR notes on Somali refugees in Ethiopia
No page opened gave a scurvy case-fatality rate or a time to death. MMWR 1989: 'Scurvy, a fatal illness if untreated', with its deaths reported only for hepatitis. Searched; null.
Plasma ascorbic acid at which non-specific, then specific, manifestations appear
micromol per L (specific manifestations); non-specific below 20

Gandhi et al. 2023: non-specific symptoms (fatigue, anorexia, irritability) 'when serum ascorbic acid concentrations dip below 20 mumol/L'; 'levels below 11.4 mumol/L indicate a substantial deficiency with which the more specific manifestations are observed'

Value is the 11.4 threshold; the 20 for non-specific symptoms is in the conditions. The page also states symptoms occur below 0.2 mg/dL, and Francescone gives low serum as under 0.1 mg/dL. The page assigns no level to wound reopening, gum disease, tooth loss or any cause of death. Cross-check with the 10 micromol per L LPI figure and the 300 mg pool in vitamin_c_depletion.
Francescone and Levitt, Cutis 76(4); Wikipedia Scurvy article

Francescone: fatigue and malaise early, myalgia as deficiency progresses, and 'late stages of scurvy are characterized by neuropathy, edema, oliguria, syncope, leukopenia, and intracerebral hemorrhage'. Wikipedia: poor wound healing 'as scurvy worsens', then death from infection or bleeding. Neither places gum disease, tooth loss or wound reopening on a named day or level.
Time in camp before clinical scurvy outbreaks among refugees on ration shortfalls
Ethiopian refugee camps, Desenclos et al. 1989, Bull WHO 67(3):309-316: 'from 3 to 4 months after their arrival'

Low 3 months and High 4 months as days (approximate). Risk 'increased significantly with the length of time that refugees had been in the camps'. Prevalence in six camps 13.6 to 44 percent. Abstract only; no signs by stage and no deaths.

rows: Periodic annual diameter growth of crop trees, 1944-61

Guanica Insular Forest, dry limestone hills of southwestern Puerto Rico; small-leaf mahogany planted 1931; 22 thriftiest, fully exposed crop trees measured 1944-61; mean temperature near 80 degF, rainfall no more than 30 in/yr; shallow heavy soils (Briscoe 1962)

The decline is attributed to competition among the trees; the trees were selected as the most vigorous, so this is a best-case rate for the stand.
Mean dbh of crop trees in 1944 (age about 13 years)

Guanica Insular Forest, dry limestone hills of southwestern Puerto Rico; small-leaf mahogany planted 1931; 22 thriftiest, fully exposed crop trees measured 1944-61; mean temperature near 80 degF, rainfall no more than 30 in/yr; shallow heavy soils (Briscoe 1962)
3.97 inch in Briscoe Table 1, converted at 2.54 cm per inch. Table text read from a scan with an OCR layer; the periodic rates in the same table agree with the differences of the four dbh values.
Mean dbh of crop trees in 1961 (age about 30 years)

Guanica Insular Forest, dry limestone hills of southwestern Puerto Rico; small-leaf mahogany planted 1931; 22 thriftiest, fully exposed crop trees measured 1944-61; mean temperature near 80 degF, rainfall no more than 30 in/yr; shallow heavy soils (Briscoe 1962)
6.35 inch in Briscoe Table 1, converted at 2.54 cm per inch. Briscoe projects 23 years to a 4-inch fence-post tree and 71 years to a 12-inch saw log at the mean 1944-61 rate.
Maximum fresh cane yield of the crop

Ayr, Queensland, Australia; autumn-planted sugarcane crop grown under irrigation; samplings 167 to 445 days after planting; cultivar, planting date, rainfall and temperature not in the opened abstract (Muchow et al. 1994)
The abstract states 'the maximum fresh cane yield was 201 t per ha', attained up to 4 months before the final sampling. The abstract gives no spread, so Low and High are null.
Maximum biomass production of the crop

Ayr, Queensland, Australia; autumn-planted sugarcane crop grown under irrigation; samplings 167 to 445 days after planting; cultivar, planting date, rainfall and temperature not in the opened abstract (Muchow et al. 1994)
The abstract states 'The maximum biomass production was 72 t per ha'. Dry or fresh basis is not stated in the abstract; read as dry biomass since the cane yield is given separately as fresh.
Maximum crop growth rate over a 140-day period

Ayr, Queensland, Australia; autumn-planted sugarcane crop grown under irrigation; samplings 167 to 445 days after planting; cultivar, planting date, rainfall and temperature not in the opened abstract (Muchow et al. 1994)
From the abstract. No spread given.
Maximum radiation use efficiency, biomass per MJ of intercepted solar radiation

Ayr, Queensland, Australia; autumn-planted sugarcane crop grown under irrigation; samplings 167 to 445 days after planting; cultivar, planting date, rainfall and temperature not in the opened abstract (Muchow et al. 1994)

The AGRIS page prints '1.75 M per J', read as g MJ-1. The abstract calls it independent of intercepted fraction and incident radiation. Basis is shortwave (total solar) radiation, not PAR, so compare it with the profile RUE only after converting by the PAR fraction (about 0.40 to 0.43 per plants.forms).
Radiation extinction coefficient from green leaf area index and intercepted fraction

Ayr, Queensland, Australia; autumn-planted sugarcane crop grown under irrigation; samplings 167 to 445 days after planting; cultivar, planting date, rainfall and temperature not in the opened abstract (Muchow et al. 1994)
From the abstract. Less than 60 percent of seasonal incident radiation was intercepted.
Mean aboveground biomass of the forest plots

Bon Accord Lagoon, southwest Tobago; fringed Rhizophora mangle forest of 0.8 km2 on the landward edge of Buccoo Reef Marine Park; seven monospecific 0.01 ha plots measured February 1998 to February 1999 (Juman 2005)

Abstract: mean 14.1 +/- 8.1 kg dry weight per m2 across plots, range 2.0 to 25.9, which are Low and High. Standing crop of the forest 11,318 +/- 6,488 t. Age and tree size per plot are not on the abstract page.
Mean litterfall rate over the year

Bon Accord Lagoon, southwest Tobago; fringed Rhizophora mangle forest of 0.8 km2 on the landward edge of Buccoo Reef Marine Park; seven monospecific 0.01 ha plots measured February 1998 to February 1999 (Juman 2005)

Abstract: 3.4 +/- 0.9 g dry weight per m2 per day, peaking May to August (4.2 to 4.3) and lowest October to December (2.3 to 2.8); Low and High are the lowest and highest seasonal means. Litterfall is an indicator of productivity, not growth itself.
Mean leaf loss rate in litterbags

Bon Accord Lagoon, southwest Tobago; fringed Rhizophora mangle forest of 0.8 km2 on the landward edge of Buccoo Reef Marine Park; seven monospecific 0.01 ha plots measured February 1998 to February 1999 (Juman 2005)
Abstract: 0.3% per day in the upper intertidal zone to 1% per day at a lower intertidal site flooded by sewage effluent, mean 0.4 +/- 1% per day (as printed).
Total biomass of Thalassia testudinum beds (leaves, shoots, rhizomes and roots)
Puerto Morelos CARICOMP site, Quintana Roo, Mexico; Thalassia testudinum beds at four seagrass sites, monitored 1993 to 2005 (Rodriguez-Martinez et al. 2010)

Abstract: total biomass ranged from 531 to 699 g dry m-2 and remained constant over the study; Low and High are those ends. The abstract gives no mean, so Value is the midpoint of the range, not a mean.
Leaf productivity of Thalassia testudinum beds
Puerto Morelos CARICOMP site, Quintana Roo, Mexico; Thalassia testudinum beds at four seagrass sites, monitored 1993 to 2005 (Rodriguez-Martinez et al. 2010)

Abstract: leaf productivity ranged from 0.89 to 1.56 g dry m-2 d-1 and remained constant; Low and High are those ends and Value is their midpoint, not a mean. The abstract names no leaf growth rate and no temperature, salinity or light values.
Share of mahogany flowers or samples in which thrips were found
West Indies mahogany, seven collecting sites in Florida 27 to 82 km apart (Howard, Nakahara and Williams 1995, as reported on an FAO page)

The FAO page says thrips were present 'in percentages which vary from 12% to 59%' across the sites and were the only insects found visiting the flowers; the abstract of the paper (seen only in search-result text) says 'in 12 to 59% of the flowers'. Low and High are the site range; Value is its midpoint, not a mean. No count per flower, no sampling dates and no pollen or fruit-set figure was opened.

excreta.title: Excreta: mass, water, nitrogen and energy of human faeces and urine per person-day, and horse faeces and urine (task 3016, integration gap CG-6)
excreta.source: Rose et al. 2015 review (PMC4500995), Cummings et al. 1992, Slavin and Marlett 1980, Miles 1988, Baer 1997, 김주연 1987, 구재옥 1988, Bingham and Cummings 1985, Viskari 2018, Saastamoinen et al. 2021, Scottish NVZ regulations 2008, Karasu and Rogers 2024. Abstracts and page text read through fetch tools; the full text of several primary papers was not opened and secondary relays are marked in the Note column.
rows: Faecal wet mass, median of study means

Review of published studies of healthy people (Rose et al. 2015, Crit Rev Environ Sci Technol; medians of study means, per person per day); the page text was read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; Section 3.1
Low and High are the lowest and highest study mean, not a spread of individuals. The text counts 116 studies, the Figure 1 caption 112.
Faecal wet mass, high-income countries, median

Review of published studies of healthy people (Rose et al. 2015, Crit Rev Environ Sci Technol; medians of study means, per person per day); the page text was read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; Table 3, n = 95
The review reports the high-income median as the baseline for the low-fibre Western diet.
Faecal wet mass, low-income countries, median

Review of published studies of healthy people (Rose et al. 2015, Crit Rev Environ Sci Technol; medians of study means, per person per day); the page text was read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; Table 3, n = 17
About double the high-income median (t = 2.87, p < .05); the review attributes it to higher fibre intake. Fibre intakes of the groups are not given in the page text read.
Faecal weight, healthy UK adults, median
220 healthy UK adults (190 with age and sex: 106 men, 84 women, mean age 39.5 y, range 18 to 80); stool collections (Cummings, Bingham, Heaton, Eastwood 1992, Gastroenterology 103:1783-1789)
Men median 104 g, women 99 g (p = 0.02). 17% of women and 1% of men passed under 50 g per day. Whole-gut transit 60 h (men 55, women 72). Mean and range are not in the abstract.
Mean faecal weight across populations worldwide (range of group means)
Other populations compiled by Cummings et al. 1992; the abstract does not list the groups
The abstract says stool weight in westernised populations is 80 to 120 g per day and was inversely related to colon cancer risk (r = -0.78).
Faecal dry mass, median of study means

Review of published studies of healthy people (Rose et al. 2015, Crit Rev Environ Sci Technol; medians of study means, per person per day); the page text was read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; Section 3.1, 60 studies
Table 3: 28 g (12 to 81, n = 57) in high-income and 38 g (18 to 62, n = 8) in low-income countries. Table 10 of the same review gives 32 g, so the review disagrees with itself by 3 g.
Dry mass as share of wet mass

Review of published studies of healthy people (Rose et al. 2015, Crit Rev Environ Sci Technol; medians of study means, per person per day); the page text was read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; n = 45
Equivalent to a water share of 75%.

Review of published studies of healthy people (Rose et al. 2015, Crit Rev Environ Sci Technol; medians of study means, per person per day); the page text was read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; Section 3.2, n = 47
Faecal water content, omnivore versus vegetarian diet (Reddy et al., as reported in Rose Table 4)
Omnivore diet with 16.6 g fibre per day gave 72.6%; vegetarian diet with 16.2 g fibre per day gave 78.9% (primary paper not opened)
Value is the omnivore figure and High the vegetarian one. At nearly equal fibre intake the vegetarian stool held more water, so water share is not a function of fibre mass alone.
Faecal nitrogen, median of study means
g N per person per day

Review of published studies of healthy people (Rose et al. 2015, Crit Rev Environ Sci Technol; medians of study means, per person per day); the page text was read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; n = 18
Nitrogen is 5 to 7% of dried solids. Faecal protein median 6.3 g per day (3.2 to 16.2, n = 7). Cross-check: 29 g dry mass at 5 to 7% N is 1.5 to 2.0 g, within the median.
Faecal nitrogen, young Korean women on a normal diet
g N per person per day
19 healthy female college students in Korea, normal diet and activity, 3-day sample collection (김주연 1987, Journal of Nutrition and Health 20(2):90-103)

The abstract gives +/- 0.10 without saying SD or SEM. Nitrogen intake by chemical analysis was 7.16 +/- 0.31 g per day, so faecal N was about 19% of intake; apparent protein digestibility 80.53 +/- 5.21%.
Faecal nitrogen per person, converted from the yearly estimate
g N per person per day
One person; Table 1 of Viskari et al. 2018 from Weckman 2005, Udert et al. 2006 and Ministry of the Environment Finland 2017; the population is not stated
Table 1 gives 0.52 kg N per person per year; 0.52 kg / 365 d = 1.42 g per day (computed here). A secondary compilation, not a measurement.
Increase in faecal wet mass per gram of dietary fibre
g wet faeces per g fibre

Review of published studies of healthy people (Rose et al. 2015, Crit Rev Environ Sci Technol; medians of study means, per person per day); the page text was read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; Figure 2 regression of wet mass on fibre intake, intercept 101.3 +/- 34.3 g

Slope is 2.96 +/- 1.13 as printed; Low and High are slope minus and plus that 1.13, which the page does not say is SE or SD. Vuksan et al. found 2.8 g per extra gram of wheat-bran fibre; Phillips et al. found 1.8 g per gram of resistant starch (both as reported by Rose).
Faecal weight at about 18 g per day of non-starch polysaccharide
Meta-analysis of 11 controlled-diet studies, 26 groups, n = 206 (Cummings et al. 1992)

The abstract says diets 'characterized by high NSP intake (approximately 18 g/day) are associated with stool weights of 150 g/day'. Fibre intake and mean stool weight correlated at r = 0.84. The regression equation is not in the abstract.
Faecal wet mass, omnivore diet with 23 g fibre per day (Davies et al., as reported in Rose Table 4)
Omnivore group of a three-diet comparison; primary paper not opened

Same comparison: vegetarian 168 g at 37 g fibre; vegan 225 g at 47 g fibre. Van Faassen et al.: omnivore 119 g wet and 27.1 g dry at 27.3 g fibre, vegetarian 189 g wet and 27.9 g dry at 40.8 g fibre, so dry mass barely moved while wet mass rose 59%.
Faecal wet mass, vegetarian diet with 37 g fibre per day (Davies et al., as reported in Rose Table 4)
Vegetarian group of the same three-diet comparison
Faecal wet mass, vegan diet with 47 g fibre per day (Davies et al., as reported in Rose Table 4)
Vegan group of the same three-diet comparison
Apparent nitrogen absorption at 44 g versus 85 g protein per day
Eight healthy Korean women, 20-day metabolic study; low protein 44 g per day, high protein 85 g per day (구재옥 1988, Journal of Nutrition and Health 21(1):47-60)

Value and Low are the low-protein diet (about 75%), High the high-protein diet (about 85%); the abstract says absorption was significantly higher on high protein and gives no faecal N in grams. So faecal N was roughly 25% of intake at 44 g protein and 15% at 85 g.
Effect of protein intake on faecal ammonia (Silvester et al., as reported in Rose)
Protein intake raised from 68 to 192 g per day; primary paper not opened
Ammonia rose from 12 to 24 mmol/kg (nitrite 829 to 1678 ug/kg). No change in faecal mass or total N is stated.

Review of published studies of healthy people (Rose et al. 2015, Crit Rev Environ Sci Technol; medians of study means, per person per day); the page text was read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; Table 10

The text gives a median of 1.4 L with a range of study means 0.6 to 2.6 L (n = 14). Fluid intake is the main driver: it explained 78% of the variation in one 11,748-day sample (Parker and Gallagher, as reported).

Review of published studies of healthy people (Rose et al. 2015, Crit Rev Environ Sci Technol; medians of study means, per person per day); the page text was read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; text, n = 7, range of means
Table 10 gives 61 g (50 to 75), so the review's own two figures differ by 2 g. Urea is over 50% of the organic solids.
g N per person per day

Review of published studies of healthy people (Rose et al. 2015, Crit Rev Environ Sci Technol; medians of study means, per person per day); the page text was read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; Table 8, n = 8
The range is wide because it spans diets and protein intakes; urinary N correlated with protein intake at r2 = 0.91 over 51 to 212 g protein per day.
Urine nitrogen per person, converted from the yearly estimate
g N per person per day
One person; Table 1 of Viskari et al. 2018 (see faeces row)

Table 1 gives 4.13 kg N per person per year; 4.13 kg / 365 d = 11.3 g per day (computed here). Urine plus faeces plus 'other' (greywater) total 5.02 kg N per year; urine is 82% of that total and 89% of urine plus faeces (computed). Lapid 2008 is quoted there for about 90% of excreted N in urine.
Urinary nitrogen, young Korean women on a normal diet
g N per person per day
19 healthy female college students, normal diet, 3-day sample (김주연 1987)

+/- 0.30 as printed, SD or SEM not stated. Urea N 4.52 +/- 0.22 g per day; creatinine 0.88 +/- 0.04 g. Nitrogen balance -0.244 +/- 0.33 g per day; faeces plus urine N (1.38 + 6.03 = 7.41 g) exceeds chemically analysed intake (7.16 g) by 0.25 g, matching the stated balance. Sweat and skin N not reported.
Urinary nitrogen as share of nitrogen intake
+/- 3.56 as printed. The authors judged the women to be in marginal protein status; a diet with surplus protein would excrete a larger share in urine (see the 44 g versus 85 g row).
Urinary nitrogen as share of dietary nitrogen (Kipnis et al., as reported in Rose)
Kipnis et al. 2003 OPEN biomarker study, 484 healthy volunteers in Maryland (primary abstract opened; it gives no recovery figure)

Rose writes 'on average, urinary N is about 80% of dietary intake'. Kipnis's own abstract only names urinary nitrogen as the reference biomarker for protein intake, so the 80% is the review's reading of the full text, which was not opened.
Day-to-day variation of urine N versus nitrogen intake within a person

Eight healthy subjects on their usual diets for 28 days, consecutive 24 h collections of urine and faeces, completeness checked with PABA and radiopaque pellets (Bingham and Cummings 1985, Am J Clin Nutr 42:1276-1289)

Within-person variation in dietary intake was 14 to 26% CV, so urine N varies less than intake. Eight verified 24 h urine collections estimated dietary N to within 81 +/- 5%. The abstract states no recovery fraction.

g urea per person per day

Review of published studies of healthy people (Rose et al. 2015, Crit Rev Environ Sci Technol; medians of study means, per person per day); the page text was read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; Table 8

Table 8 gives 10 to 35 g (Bender and Bender) and 1.36 to 6.77 g (Calloway and Margen); no median. Urea nitrogen is the nitrogen mass share of urea (two N of molar mass 14.007 in 60.06 g/mol, 46.6%, computed here), so 35 g of urea is 16 g N, above the median total N of 11 g (Table 8's total-N range itself runs to 35 g).
Urea nitrogen as share of total urinary nitrogen
Urea nitrogen as share of urinary nitrogen at 44 g versus 85 g protein per day
Eight Korean women, low protein 44 g per day to high protein 85 g per day (구재옥 1988)
Value and Low are the low-protein diet, High the high-protein diet. The abstract says urinary N rose with protein intake but gives no grams.

Review of published studies of healthy people (Rose et al. 2015, Crit Rev Environ Sci Technol; medians of study means, per person per day); the page text was read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; n = 14

7 young women, control diet low in cellulose (Slavin and Marlett 1980, J Nutr 110:2020-2026)
Computed here as 100 - 95.4% gross-energy digestibility; the abstract gives only digestibility, not faecal energy, and assumes digestibility is the apparent (intake minus faecal) kind.

Same 7 women in a second month with 16 g per day Solka Floc added

Computed as 100 - 92.0% digestibility (p < 0.01). Undigested faecal fibre was the major source of the extra faecal energy; with the fibre energy subtracted, digestibility was 96.1% versus 95.6% (no meaningful difference). Fat digestibility 96.3 versus 95.4%, nitrogen 93.2 versus 92.9%, both no effect.
Overestimate of metabolizable energy by Atwater specific factors, 37 g fibre diet

12 men on two crossover diets of natural foods, 6 weeks each, 2,800 kcal menus; diet 1 had 37 g total dietary fibre from fruit and vegetables, diet 2 had 16 g from juices (Miles, Kelsay and Wong 1988, J Nutr 118:1075-1081)
Diet 2 (16 g fibre) was overestimated by 4.6%. The abstract says energy and nutrient availability were lower on the higher-fibre diet but gives no faecal energy or digestibility numbers.
Effect of dietary fibre on metabolizable energy and digestibility of mixed diets

17 subjects, three of nine diets each for 14 days, 5-day urine and faeces collection; fat 18, 34 or 47% of energy, fibre 3, 4 or 7% of diet dry matter (Baer, Rumpler, Miles and Fahey 1997, J Nutr 127:579-586)

Abstract: 'increasing fiber intake decreased fat and protein digestibility' so metabolizable energy fell as fibre rose; total and neutral-detergent fibre had similar effects. No energy digestibility, faecal energy or kcal values are in the abstract; the full text was not opened.

Six Finnhorse mares, mean initial body weight 565 +/- 30.0 kg; 6 x 4 Latin square, four 3-week periods, 17 days preliminary feeding then 4-day total faeces and urine collection; diets A haylage only, B hay only, C hay 70% + oats 30% (Saastamoinen et al. 2021, Animals 11:3568); Tables 5 and 6
Value is hay only (B), Low hay plus oats (C), High haylage only (A). Dry matter intake 8.09, 7.52 and 8.06 kg per day for B, A and C.

Value is hay only (B); A 52, C 43. Nitrogen intake (Table 3) was about 0.14, 0.11 and 0.12 kg per day for A, B and C, given to two decimals only.

g N per horse per day

Six Finnhorse mares, mean initial body weight 565 +/- 30.0 kg; 6 x 4 Latin square, four 3-week periods, 17 days preliminary feeding then 4-day total faeces and urine collection; diets A haylage only, B hay only, C hay 70% + oats 30% (Saastamoinen et al. 2021, Animals 11:3568); Table 5

Urinary N exceeded faecal N on every diet.

Six Finnhorse mares, mean initial body weight 565 +/- 30.0 kg; 6 x 4 Latin square, four 3-week periods, 17 days preliminary feeding then 4-day total faeces and urine collection; diets A haylage only, B hay only, C hay 70% + oats 30% (Saastamoinen et al. 2021, Animals 11:3568); Tables 3 and 5

Intake on B is about 110 g, so excretion exceeds intake on every diet; the authors did not compute N balance 'because of the uncertain urine collection method and calculated values'. Mass balance does not close in the source itself.
Daily excreta and nitrogen, horse, regulatory standard
L of excreta per animal per day
Schedule 1, Table 1 of The Action Programme for Nitrate Vulnerable Zones (Scotland) Regulations 2008, 'Standards for the volume of excreta and nitrogen in manure produced by livestock'
The same row gives 58 g N per animal per day. No body weight, diet, or split of faeces and urine is stated. For comparison a dairy cow of over 9,000 L milk per year is 64 L and 315 g N per day.
Daily nitrogen production, horse, regulatory standard
g N per animal per day
Same table and row as the excreta volume
Less than half of the faeces plus urine N measured on a 565 kg mare eating hay only (about 136 g unacidified).

g N per horse per day
Online survey of 274 horse owners in the Netherlands, mean horse weight 542.4 +/- 101.9 kg (Karasu and Rogers 2024, J Equine Vet Sci 137:105071)

228 +/- 134 as printed (Low and High are that value minus and plus 134, not a measured range); equal to 8.47 kg N per tonne of manure. A calculation from reported feeding practice, not a measurement of excreta; the abstract does not give the formula or the faeces and urine mass.

gut_fermentation.title: Gut microbial digestion: fibre fermented, energy recovered as short-chain fatty acids, the gas made, and the horse and ruminant compared (task 3017, integration gap CG-10)
gut_fermentation.source: FAO/WHO Paper 66 (1998), Hervik and Svihus 2019, Elia and Cummings 2007, McNeil 1984, Bergman 1990, Cummings et al 1987, McNeil et al 1978, Boets et al 2015, NIST WebBook, Christl et al 1992, Strocchi and Levitt 1992, Mahmood et al 2020, Santo et al 2026, Zicarelli et al 2023, Ebert and Moore-Colyer 2020, Rutgers extension. Abstracts and page text read through fetch tools; where a figure is relayed from a study not opened, the Note column says so. Rows marked derived are my arithmetic from other rows.
rows: Energy value set for carbohydrate that reaches the colon, for nutrition and labelling
FAO/WHO Expert Consultation, Rome 14 to 18 April 1997 (FAO Food and Nutrition Paper 66, 1998), Recommendation 8; page text read

Printed as 2 kcal/g (8 kJ/g). The same recommendation asks that the energy value of all dietary carbohydrate be reassessed with modern techniques. The recommendation text says nothing of fermentation, short-chain fatty acids or resistant starch.
Fraction of undigestible carbohydrate that is fermented
FAO Food and Nutrition Paper 66, Annex 2, 'Digestion, absorption and energy value of carbohydrates'; page text read

Value null: the page gives only a range, that the fermented share 'may vary from 0 to 100%'. It names energy lost 'in the gases and heat produced during colonic fermentation' but gives no amount for gas, heat or bacterial mass.
Digestible energy value of fibre across human studies (Livesey's review, as quoted)
Narrative review (Hervik and Svihus 2019, J Nutr Metab), section 5.3, quoting Livesey's review; page text read

Value null: a range, 'varied from -20 to +10 kJ/g'. The abstract adds that the net energy of soluble, non-viscous, easily fermented fibres can exceed 10 kJ/g and that many fibres fall 'well below' the 8 kJ/g used on labels. A negative value means the fibre carried more energy out in faeces than it brought in.
Net energy value, sugar beet fibre
Healthy human subjects; relayed by Hervik and Svihus 2019 (section 5.3); the original study was not opened
Metabolizable energy of the same fibre was 10.7 kJ/g in the review's wording. The two numbers differ because net energy counts the heat and losses of fermentation and metabolizable energy does not.
Healthy human subjects; relayed by Hervik and Svihus 2019 (section 5.3); the original study was not opened
Metabolizable energy of the same fibre was 13.0 kJ/g in the review's wording.
Net energy value, fibre from coarse rye bread
Human study; relayed by Hervik and Svihus 2019 (section 5.3); the original study was not opened
Negative, so the fibre cost the body energy. The review gives 4.9 kJ/g for whole rye bread when only fermentation is counted.
Net energy value, citrus fibre (faecal-loss basis)
Human study; relayed by Hervik and Svihus 2019 (section 5.3); the original study was not opened
Computed from faecal energy loss, per the review.
Apparent digestibility of dietary fibre in humans, Wisker et al.
Human feeding study; relayed by Hervik and Svihus 2019 (section 5.3); the original study was not opened
Apparent means intake minus faecal recovery, so it counts fermented fibre plus any fibre that was lost in other ways; it is not a direct fermentation measurement.
Apparent faecal digestibility of dietary fibre in humans, Baer et al.
Human feeding studies; relayed by Hervik and Svihus 2019 (section 5.3); the original study was not opened
Value null: the review gives 'between 67 and 82 percent'. Same limits as the Wisker figure; the two studies differ by fibre source and diet, which this relay does not give.
Westernised diets; Elia and Cummings 2007 review abstract (Eur J Clin Nutr 61 Suppl 1:S40-74), read through Europe PMC

Value null: a range. The abstract says it 'may reach about 50 g/day' in populations on largely cereal staples or high fruit and vegetable diets. Gives amount arriving, not how much is fermented. Abstract only; the full text sits behind a login.
Short-chain fatty acid production in the human colon
Review statement (Hervik and Svihus 2019 section 5.1; citation for the figure not seen)
Worked in the review as about 20 g of acids per day at an assumed acetate:propionate:butyrate molar ratio of 2.0:0.5:0.5.
In vitro short-chain fatty acid yield per 100 g fibre, range across fibre types
In vitro fermentations as summarised by Hervik and Svihus 2019, section 5.1
Value null: 'as low as 10 g per 100 g for pea hulls, oat hulls and cellulose to 40 g for pectins'. An in vitro yield, not a human fermented fraction.
Total short-chain fatty acids in colon contents, caecum
Sudden-death victims, samples within 4 h of death (Cummings et al 1987, Gut 28:1221-7); abstract read through Europe PMC

Low is the descending colon (80 +/- 11); the caecum is 131 +/- 9. The terminal ileum held 13 +/- 6. Concentration fell steadily from caecum to descending colon while pH rose from 5.6 to 6.6. Autopsy contents show concentration, not production rate.
Total short-chain fatty acids in portal blood

Low is peripheral venous blood (79 +/- 22); hepatic vein 148 +/- 42; portal 375 +/- 70. Acetate was the main anion throughout. The molar ratios shifted from colon to portal to hepatic blood, which the authors read as the colon wall taking up more butyrate and the liver more propionate.
Net absorption rate of acetate from the human rectum, mixed acid solution
46 obesity-clinic patients, dialysis-bag technique (McNeil, Cummings and James 1978, Gut 19:819-22); abstract read

In a mixed electrolyte solution acetate absorption was 8.1. Lowering pH from 7.2 to 5.5 did not change rates, so the authors judged it not passive diffusion of the undissociated acid. Rectum, not colon.
Net absorption rate of propionate from the human rectum, mixed acid solution
Net absorption rate of butyrate from the human rectum, mixed acid solution
Share of colonic short-chain fatty acids excreted in faeces
Introduction of Boets et al 2015 (Nutrients 7:8916-29), a general statement with no citation seen on the page read
Value null: 'only 5%-10% is excreted in feces'. A secondary relay in a paper that measured something else.
Share of colonic acids reaching the systemic circulation, used as an assumption
Boets et al 2015, model assumptions for 12 healthy adults

Value null: the paper assumed 40% of colonic acetate, 10% of propionate and 5% of butyrate reach the systemic circulation, taken from literature, 'not measurements', and the authors name this their major limitation.
Colonic acetate produced per g inulin (model-derived)
12 healthy adults, 15 g inulin with breakfast, 12 h (Boets et al 2015); production estimated from blood appearance and the assumptions above, not measured in the colon
Total over 12 h was 137 +/- 75 mmol. The amount of inulin actually fermented was not measured.
Colonic propionate produced per g inulin (model-derived)
Colonic butyrate produced per g inulin (model-derived)
Total over 12 h was 20 +/- 17 mmol. Molar ratio acetate:propionate:butyrate was 82:6:12.
Share of human energy needs supplied by large-intestine fermentation
Review (McNeil 1984, Am J Clin Nutr 39:338-42); abstract read through Europe PMC
Value null: a range. The abstract says smaller amounts may come from fat absorbed in the large intestine and from bacterial breakdown products of protein.
Energy contribution of volatile fatty acids, humans
Review (Bergman 1990, Physiol Rev 70:567-90); abstract read through Europe PMC
Stated as 'about 10% for humans'. The abstract says higher fibre intake likely raises production and the share.
Energy contribution of volatile fatty acids, ruminants (sheep, cattle)
Stated as 'about 70%'. This is the foregut-fermenter figure; the abstract does not say whether it is of maintenance, digestible or metabolizable energy.
Energy contribution of volatile fatty acids, several other omnivorous or herbivorous species

Value null: 'about 20-30%'. The abstract read does not name which species; a search summary of the paper said ponies and rabbits were highest, but that was not on the page opened, so the horse is not placed here.
Value null: 'from about 75:15:10 to 40:40:20'. Higher propionate share goes with more starch-like substrate in other literature, which this abstract does not say.
Where absorbed short-chain fatty acids are used

Value null. Absorbed quickly where formed; the gut wall metabolises much before the portal blood (most butyrate to ketone bodies or CO2); the liver removes nearly all the rest of the butyrate and takes up propionate, much of it made into glucose; acetate is used mainly by peripheral tissues such as fat and muscle, with species differences. Bicarbonate release accompanies absorption.
Enthalpy of combustion of acetic acid, liquid
Liquid acid at standard state, NIST WebBook (Steele, Chirico et al 1997, J Chem Eng Data 42:1052)
Low and High are the printed +/- 0.34. Liquid acid, not the dissolved ion in blood or gut contents.
Enthalpy of combustion of propionic acid, liquid
Liquid acid at standard state, NIST WebBook (Lebedeva 1964)
Low and High are the printed +/- 0.1. A second value in the table (Schjanberg 1935) reads -1528.
Enthalpy of combustion of butyric acid, liquid
Liquid acid at standard state, NIST WebBook (Lebedeva 1964)
Low and High are the printed +/- 0.59.
Combustion energy of the acids made per g inulin (derived)
My arithmetic (task 3017): 9.13 x 875.16 + 0.72 x 1527.3 + 1.31 x 2183.5 per g, from the Boets yields and the NIST enthalpies

A derived value, not a finding of either source: it mixes a model-derived yield with liquid-phase enthalpies and ignores acids lost in faeces, the heat of fermentation and any inulin left unfermented. Its closeness to the 11.9 kJ/g net energy of inulin (Hervik) is a consistency check, not a proof.
Combustion energy of 300 mmol per day of acids at ratio 2.0:0.5:0.5 (derived)
My arithmetic (task 3017): 200 mmol acetate, 50 propionate, 50 butyrate x the NIST enthalpies
About 4% of a 2,000 kcal (8,368 kJ) day, taken here as a reference only. Below the 5 to 10% in McNeil and the 10% in Bergman, so the 300 mmol figure and the review shares do not match exactly.
Hydrogen excreted per g lactulose, subjects who do not excrete methane
10 healthy adults in a whole-body calorimeter, 7.5, 15 and 22.5 g lactulose (Christl, Murgatroyd, Gibson, Cummings 1992, Gastroenterology 102:1269); abstract read
Excreted H2 (breath plus flatus), net of what the gut bacteria consumed. Not the amount produced.
Hydrogen excreted per g lactulose, subjects who also excrete methane
Same study (4 of 10 subjects were methane excretors)
The abstract gives 34.9 mL/g for hydrogen plus methane together and does not say for which subjects.
Hydrogen plus methane excreted per g lactulose
Methane doses: 51.3, 97.3 and 157.5 mL at 7.5, 15 and 22.5 g lactulose in the four methane excretors; hydrogen 88.1, 227.0 and 321.8 mL in all ten.
Hydrogen excreted after 20 g pectin, as a share of an equal dose of lactulose
+/- 3.2. Pectin is fermented but gives little hydrogen, so hydrogen excretion cannot stand in for fermentation.
Hydrogen excreted after 22.2 g banana starch, as a share of an equal dose of lactulose
Total hydrogen excretion on a starch- and fibre-free diet
Share of excreted hydrogen and methane that leaves in the breath
Up to 200 mL per 24 h of total excretion 65% was exhaled; above that 25%; the overall average was 58%. The rest leaves as flatus. The authors call this higher than previously accepted.
Fate of hydrogen made in the colon
Same study (Christl et al 1992), faecal incubations

Value null. 'Substantial amounts of H2 are consumed by methanogenic and sulfate-reducing bacteria.' Sulfate reduction was 58.7 +/- 5.6 nmol per h per g wet faeces in non-methanogens against 7.9 +/- 2.0 in methanogens; acetogenesis was very low in both.
Absolute hydrogen production by human faecal flora fermenting glucose, at low hydrogen pressure
In vitro incubation of human faeces (Strocchi and Levitt 1992, J Clin Invest 89:1304-11); abstract read through PMC
At high and intermediate hydrogen pressure net production was only 1/900 and 1/64 of the absolute figure, because the flora consume most of what it makes. The abstract gives no methane or CO2 yield.
Textbook balance in Table 1 of Mahmood et al 2020 (Archaea), a rumen in vitro paper; [2H] is a hydrogen pair
C6H12O6 + 2 H2O -> 2 CH3COOH + 4 [2H] + 2 CO2. Rumen paper, not the colon; a 1993 pig paper says the rumen and hindgut share nearly the same pathways, which was read only as a search summary.
C6H12O6 + 2 [2H] -> 2 CH3CH2COOH + 2 H2O. Uses hydrogen; makes no CO2.
CO2 released by the acid balances per g inulin before methanogenesis (derived)
My arithmetic (task 3017): 1 CO2 per acetate and 2 per butyrate from the balances above, times the Boets yields: 9.13 + 2 x 1.31

Derived. Assumes each acid forms by the single balance above, so no lactate, succinate or biomass; the same balances give a net 18.85 mmol [2H] per g (acetate +2, butyrate +1, propionate -1 each), which methanogenesis alone could turn into at most 4.7 mmol CH4 per g. The measured methane plus hydrogen was about 1.4 mmol per g lactulose (34.9 mL/g divided by an ideal-gas molar volume of about 24.5 mL per mmol, my conversion), so most hydrogen goes elsewhere (sulfate reduction, other sinks).
Total short-chain fatty acids in horse caecal contents
23 horses (471 +/- 63 kg) on pasture, hay, or hay with oats, pooled (Santo et al 2026, PLoS One, Table 4); page text read to about 100,000 characters
Acetate 59.4, propionate 17.0, n-butyrate 6.3. Pasture had the highest total (P = 0.006 against hay); rations are not split in the text. Concentration, not production.
Total short-chain fatty acids in horse ventral colon contents (dextrum)
Acetate 79.6, propionate 21.3, n-butyrate 10.8. The highest of the segments, with the sinistrum part at 109.6.
Total short-chain fatty acids in horse rectal contents
Acetate 33.3, propionate 7.1, n-butyrate 2.1. Dorsal colon about 93; transverse colon 61.5, so concentration falls toward the rectum.
Acetate:propionate:butyrate in horse ventral colon, calculated
From Table 4 pooled means (my arithmetic, task 3017: 79.6 : 21.3 : 10.8)
About 3.7 : 1 : 0.5. The paper states only the (acetate + butyrate)/propionate ratio, 3.8 to 4.3 in caecum and ventral colon, 5.0 to 5.5 from dorsal colon to rectum.
Share of horse maintenance energy covered by short-chain fatty acids, discussion statement
Discussion of Santo et al 2026, citing refs 46 and 47 which were not opened
Value null: 'Horses are capable to cover 60-70% of their energy maintenance requirements through SCFA'. A claim relayed from sources not read; it is not about the hindgut alone.
Share of horse energy needs met by hindgut short-chain fatty acids, extension page
Rutgers Cooperative Extension fact sheet E375; page text read
Value null: '50-70% of a horse's energy needs are met by SCFAs absorbed from the hindgut'. The sentence carries no citation; the nearby references belong to other claims.
Apparent crude fibre digestibility in horses, whole tract, five hay and concentrate diets
4 horses, 6 years, 500 +/- 22 kg, forage:concentrate 90:10 to 50:50, dry matter intake 10.7 to 11.2 kg/day (Zicarelli et al 2023, Animals, Table 3)

Value null: a range across diets. Organic matter digestibility ran 46.7 to 65.5%. Whole-tract figure, so it does not say how much was digested in the hindgut. The paper reports no energy digestibility.
Gas obtained per mmol of volatile fatty acid, in vitro fermentation of horse diets
In vitro gas test on the five diets (Zicarelli et al 2023, section 3.2); the inoculum and gas composition were not read
The gas is mostly CO2 plus some methane and hydrogen; the page gives no split.
Methane energy deducted per g crude fibre when converting horse digestible to metabolizable energy
Equation used in a study of performance horses (Ebert and Moore-Colyer 2020, Transl Anim Sci); cites Kienzle and Zeyner 2010 and Hipp et al 2017
Printed as 0.002 MJ. An estimate applied by the authors, not a measurement. The same paper says digestible-energy systems overstate forage energy by about 15% (citing INRA 2012).
