Energy deposited in new tissue per day, infants 11 to 12 months
FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome 17-24 October 2001 (Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series 1, 2004); page text read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; Table 3.2
Boys 93 kJ/day and girls 60 kJ/day (printed as 0.093 and 0.06 MJ/day, converted by me). All twelve monthly rows of the table were read; four are kept here.
Growth energy as a share of total energy requirement, first 3 months of life
FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome 17-24 October 2001 (Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series 1, 2004); page text read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; chapter 3 section 3.3

About 35% over months 0 to 3, 40% in the first month, 17.5% over months 3 to 6, under 6% over months 6 to 12. Section 3.4.2 gives about 23% for the third month alone, which sits under the 35% average and is not a conflict.
Growth energy as a share of total energy requirement, months 3 to 6
FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome 17-24 October 2001 (Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series 1, 2004); page text read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; chapter 3 section 3.3
Growth energy as a share of total energy requirement at 12 months
FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome 17-24 October 2001 (Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series 1, 2004); page text read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; chapter 3 section 3.3

Under 2% in the second year. A search summary of the Australian 'Eat for Health' page (not opened) says the same report gives 5% at 12 months; the report's chapter 3 text, as read, says about 3%. The report is taken as the source.
Growth energy as a share of total energy requirement, childhood to mid-adolescence
FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome 17-24 October 2001 (Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series 1, 2004); page text read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; chapter 3 section 3.3
1 to 2% until mid-adolescence, disappearing by about age 20.
Average energy deposited per g of weight gain, children and adolescents
kJ per g of weight gain
FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome 17-24 October 2001 (Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series 1, 2004); page text read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; chapter 4 section 4.3

Printed as 2 kcal/g. The report assumes growing tissue is 10% fat and 20% protein, the remaining 70% negligible. Check: 0.10 x 38.7 + 0.20 x 23.6 = 8.6 kJ/g (my arithmetic). The text says even a 50% error in this value changes requirements by about 1%.
Growth energy as a share of total energy requirement, children 1 to 18 years

FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome 17-24 October 2001 (Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series 1, 2004); page text read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; derived by the fetch summary from the deposition column and the requirement columns of Tables 4.2 and 4.3, not printed as a percent
Low and High are the extremes the summary found: about 1.4 to 1.6% at 1 to 2 years, about 1% for most ages to 16, near 0 by 17 to 18. Treat as an arithmetic check, not a quoted figure.
Allowance for the energy cost of growth, per g of weight gain
kJ per g of weight gain
Waterlow, The Energy Cost of Growth, Joint FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation 1981 (FAO document M2885E), section 3; page text read through a page-fetch summary

Printed as 5 kcal/g; the kJ is my conversion (x 4.184). This is energy stored plus synthesis, so it is higher than the stored-only 8.6 kJ/g that the 2004 report adds to total expenditure for children. The 1981 paper is the older basis.
Energy cost of depositing 1 g fat (stored plus synthesis)
Waterlow 1981 section 1.2; figure comes from pig and lamb studies, not infants
Printed as 12.0 kcal/g; kJ is my conversion. For comparison the fat stores 38.7 kJ/g, so the synthesis part is about 11.5 kJ/g (my subtraction).
Energy cost of depositing 1 g protein (stored plus synthesis)
Waterlow 1981 section 1.2; figure comes from pig and lamb studies, not infants

Printed as 8.7 kcal/g; kJ is my conversion. Protein stores 23.6 kJ/g, so the synthesis part is about 12.8 kJ/g (my subtraction). The text adds that infant and piglet data suggest 0.5 to 1 g of extra protein is synthesised per g deposited.
Energy going to tissue gain as a share of intake, newborn
Waterlow 1981 Table 1 (infants); 10 g/kg/day birth gain assumed
Falls to about 6.4% at 6 months and 2.6% at 12 months in the same table. The 2004 report's shares (35%, 17.5%, 3%) are for deposition, from newer measurements.
Thermoneutral ambient temperature range, nude, resting at basal rate
Kingma, Frijns, Schellen, van Marken Lichtenbelt 2014, Temperature 1(2):142-149; biophysical model of an adult, core 37 degC, results section; page text read through a fetch summary

A model result, not a measurement. The discussion gives the lower bound as 26.4 degC, so the paper is inconsistent by 0.5 degC. The lower bound is the lower critical temperature of a nude resting person.
Thermoneutral ambient temperature range, clothed, seated office work
Kingma et al 2014 model, results section
A later section gives the lower bound as 14.5 degC. The clothing insulation used was not read.
Basal heat production inside the nude thermoneutral zone
Kingma et al 2014 model; about 46 W per m2 of skin
A model input range for the person modelled. Seated clothed office work is about 112 W (106 to 118 W), about 60 W per m2.
Mean skin temperature range inside the nude thermoneutral zone
Kingma et al 2014 model; core temperature allowed 36 to 38 degC; clothed skin range 28.8 to 36.4 degC
Comfortable skin range quoted from Gagge: 31.5 to 35.5 degC.
Non-shivering thermogenesis as a fraction of metabolic rate in the model
Kingma et al 2014 model, equation 'Mnst = 0.12 M'

A modelling assumption of the paper, not a measurement. Stages in the paper: sweating when heat loss is below production, then non-shivering thermogenesis, then shivering plus non-shivering. The paper gives no continuous curve of metabolic rate against ambient temperature below the lower critical temperature.
Maximum cold-induced heat production (shivering plus non-shivering) in the model
Kingma et al 2014 model, called the empirical maximum
About 4.3 times the 86 W basal rate (my division). The source of the 372 W was not given in the text read.
Shivering heat production predicted from core and mean skin temperature

Tikuisis and Giesbrecht 1999, Eur J Appl Physiol 79:221-229; 14 men (28 +/- 5 y, 77.7 +/- 6.9 kg, body fat 18.4 +/- 4.5%) in water down to 8 degC for up to 1 h, then rewarmed shivering; 3343 observations, core 35.92 +/- 0.93 degC, skin 23.4 +/- 8.9 degC; abstract read

Best model: Mshiv = [155.5 x (37 - Tc) + 47.0 x (33 - Ts) - 1.57 x (33 - Ts)^2] / (%BF)^0.5, with Tc core and Ts mean skin in degC and %BF body fat percent. Valid for Tc 33.25 to about 38 degC. The abstract does not say whether Mshiv counts the resting rate or only the extra, nor whether the terms are clipped at zero above the set points. Full text was not opened.
Shivering heat per degree of core cooling below 37 degC (before the body-fat divisor)
Divided by the square root of body fat percent. At 18.4% body fat the divisor is 4.29 (my arithmetic).
Shivering heat per degree of skin cooling below 33 degC, linear term

The quadratic term is -1.57 W per m2 per degC squared, so the skin effect peaks near 33 - 47.0/(2 x 1.57) = 18 degC (my arithmetic), in line with the abstract's remark that skin thermosensitivity is parabolic, peaking near 20 degC (Benzinger 1969).
Metabolic heat production with skin clamped at 31 degC, cold-exposed adults
Dumont et al 2022, Am J Physiol Regul Integr Comp Physiol; 12 men and 12 women; abstract read
Mean +/- SD 5.2 +/- 1.2 kJ/min, about 87 W (my conversion). Shivering 0.6 +/- 0.1 % of maximal voluntary contraction. The cold exposure used to hold the skin temperature was not in the abstract.
Metabolic heat production with skin clamped at 29 degC, cold-exposed adults
Dumont et al 2022; 12 men and 12 women; abstract read
Mean +/- SD 5.9 +/- 1.5 kJ/min, about 98 W (my conversion). Shivering 1.1 +/- 0.4 % MVC.
Metabolic heat production with skin clamped at 27 degC, cold-exposed adults
Dumont et al 2022; 12 men and 12 women; abstract read
Mean +/- SD 7.0 +/- 1.8 kJ/min, about 117 W (my conversion), 35% above the 31 degC value (my arithmetic). Shivering 2.5 +/- 0.7 % MVC.
Non-shivering thermogenesis in mild cold, as a share of resting metabolic rate
Review, J Physiol Anthropol 2025 (PMC11837704, first 100,000 of 278,348 characters read); one cited study at 18.6 degC for 90 min
Mean 13.5% in that study. At 19 degC about 5% of RMR in people with little brown fat and about 18% in people with much. Between-person spread is as large as the mean.
Printed as about five times RMR and 40 to 50% of maximal oxygen uptake. Compare the 4.3 x basal in the Kingma model.
Brown fat share of non-shivering thermogenesis
Review, J Physiol Anthropol 2025 (PMC11837704); two PET-based estimates

The text gives about 5% in one study and about 1% (neck and upper chest) in another, and also 'almost 0 to 16% of RMR, accounting for 90% of NST' in a third. The estimates conflict and the review does not reconcile them.
Shivering threshold temperature, South Asian against Caucasian adults
Printed as 'approximately 2 degC higher on average'. Which temperature (skin or ambient) was not stated in the passage read.
Lower critical temperature of cold-housed weanling horses
Autio, Sihto, Mononen, Heiskanen 2008, Agric Food Sci 17:338-350; 10 weanlings 6 to 12 months old, loose housing, November to March, central Finland

The paper takes -11 degC from earlier studies and finds it holds in early winter by comparing intake above and below it. Other values it cites: growing horses 0 degC (1 to 2% more digestible energy per degC below), mature horses -15 degC (2.5% more metabolizable energy per degC below, McBride et al 1985, relayed).
Increase in metabolizable energy intake per degC of cooling, weanling horses, November

0.5% per degC in December, 0.2% in January, none in February and March. The paper reads the fall as the horses growing and acclimatising (more insulation). A drop to -20 degC raised energy need about 18% in November, 5% in December, 2% in January.
Total energy cost of pregnancy, mean weight gain 12 kg

FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome 17-24 October 2001 (Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series 1, 2004); page text read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; chapter 6 Table 6.3 and section 6.3

Printed as 77,000 kcal. The BMR-based method gives 322.6 MJ and the total-energy-expenditure-based method 320.2 MJ; 321 is the average. The 1981 theoretical estimate was 335 MJ. Weight gain range 10 to 14 kg.
Extra energy per day, first trimester (12 kg weight gain)
FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome 17-24 October 2001 (Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series 1, 2004); page text read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; chapter 6 section 6.3
Printed as 85 kcal/day. BMR-based 421 kJ/day, TEE-based 287 kJ/day (Table 6.3B and 6.3C).
Extra energy per day, second trimester (12 kg weight gain)
FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome 17-24 October 2001 (Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series 1, 2004); page text read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; chapter 6 section 6.3
Printed as 285 kcal/day. BMR-based 1235 kJ/day, TEE-based 1112 kJ/day. For women who start prenatal care late the report advises +1.5 MJ/day (360 kcal) in this trimester.
Extra energy per day, third trimester (12 kg weight gain)
FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome 17-24 October 2001 (Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series 1, 2004); page text read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; chapter 6 section 6.3
Printed as 475 kcal/day. BMR-based 1845 kJ/day, TEE-based 2075 kJ/day.
Pregnancy rise in basal metabolic rate, over the pre-pregnancy rate

FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome 17-24 October 2001 (Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series 1, 2004); page text read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; chapter 6 sections 6.2.2 and Table 6.1
About 5%, 10% and 25% in the first, second and third trimesters. Cumulative increase 154 MJ at 12.5 kg gain (about 148 MJ at 12 kg).
Pregnancy rise in total energy expenditure by the third trimester
FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome 17-24 October 2001 (Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series 1, 2004); page text read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; chapter 6 Table 6.2
TEE increments of 85, 350 and 1300 kJ/day per trimester for 12 kg gain (section 6.2.3).
Protein deposited over pregnancy, 12 kg weight gain
FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome 17-24 October 2001 (Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series 1, 2004); page text read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; chapter 6 Table 6.3A
At 23.6 kJ/g this is about 14.1 MJ (my arithmetic).
Fat deposited over pregnancy, 12 kg weight gain
FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome 17-24 October 2001 (Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series 1, 2004); page text read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; chapter 6 Table 6.3A

At 38.7 kJ/g this is about 144.8 MJ (my arithmetic). With protein 158.9 MJ stored; divided by the 0.90 efficiency of energy use (Table 6.3 footnote b) that is 176.6 MJ, and plus the 148 MJ BMR rise gives about 325 MJ, near the printed 321 MJ.
Efficiency of energy utilisation for tissue deposition in pregnancy
FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome 17-24 October 2001 (Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series 1, 2004); page text read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; chapter 6 Table 6.3 footnote b
The 10% loss is the synthesis cost here, so the deposition term is stored energy divided by 0.90.
Total energy cost of pregnancy, mean weight gain 12.0 kg
Butte and King 2005, Public Health Nutr 8(7A):1010-1027; review; abstract and full text read

Distributed as 375, 1200 and 1950 kJ/day over the first, second and third trimesters. For a 13.8 kg gain of well-nourished women the same method gave 374 MJ (BMR-based) or 369 MJ (TEE-based), about 430, 1375 and 2245 kJ/day.
Extra energy per day, first trimester (12.0 kg weight gain)
Extra energy per day, second trimester (12.0 kg weight gain)
Extra energy per day, third trimester (12.0 kg weight gain)
Rise in total energy expenditure (doubly labelled water), by trimester
Butte and King 2005, section on TEE

0.1, 0.4 and 1.5 MJ/day in the first, second and third trimesters (1, 6 and 19% over baseline) while body weight rose 2, 8 and 18%. BMR rose 2, 9 and 24%. Activity energy expenditure changed by about -2, 3 and 6%. Average BMR rise across studies 157 MJ in total, 4.5, 10.8 and 24.0% by trimester.
Share of the protein deposited in pregnancy that goes to each tissue
Butte and King 2005, section on protein and fat accretion

Foetus 42%, uterus 17%, blood 14%, placenta 10%, breasts 8% (sums to 91%; the remainder is not named in the text read). Protein deposition falls 20% in the second and 80% in the third trimester. Fat accretion averages 8 g/day in the first and 26 g/day in the second trimester; the third is very variable (the lower end is garbled in the text read). Fat distribution over trimesters 11, 47 and 42%.
Rise in basal metabolic rate per gestational week, measured
Butte, Wong, Treuth, Ellis, O'Brian Smith 2004, Am J Clin Nutr 79:1078-1087; 63 women (17 low, 34 normal, 12 high BMI) measured at 0, 9, 22, 36 weeks; abstract read through a fetch summary
Standard deviation 5.4. Total energy expenditure rose 5.2 +/- 12.8 kcal per week, so activity energy expenditure fell slightly. About 45 kJ per week for BMR (my conversion).
Extra energy requirement, second trimester, normal-BMI women (measured plus deposition)

About 1.46 MJ/day (my conversion). The first trimester is 'negligible'; the third is 500 kcal/day (about 2.09 MJ/day). Compare FAO's 285 and 475 kcal/day. Protein deposited averaged 611 g; fat 5.3, 4.6 and 8.4 kg in the low, normal and high BMI groups (P = 0.02).
Extra energy requirement, third trimester, normal-BMI women (measured plus deposition)
Milk intake of exclusively breastfed infants, mean of months 1 to 6
FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome 17-24 October 2001 (Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series 1, 2004); page text read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; chapter 7 Table 7.2
By month 699, 731, 751, 780, 796, 854 g/day. Corrected for insensible water loss the mean is 807 g/day. Partial breastfeeding after 6 months averages 550 g/day.
FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome 17-24 October 2001 (Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series 1, 2004); page text read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; chapter 7 section 7.1.2
Printed as 0.67 kcal/g, a mean from 1 to 24 months of lactation.
Efficiency of converting food energy into milk energy
FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome 17-24 October 2001 (Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series 1, 2004); page text read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; chapter 7 section 7.1.3
The report applies 80%; the biochemical efficiency is estimated at 80 to 85%. The 20% loss is heat, and in the engine it is the extra heat of lactation.
FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome 17-24 October 2001 (Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series 1, 2004); page text read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; chapter 7 Table 7.2
Monthly costs 2569, 2686, 2760, 2867, 2925 and 3138 kJ/day, mean 2824 kJ/day (675 kcal). Milk energy 769 g x 2.8 kJ/g is 2.15 MJ and 2.15 / 0.80 is 2.69 MJ, close to the 2.8 MJ (my arithmetic).
Energy cost of partial breastfeeding (550 g/day of milk)
FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome 17-24 October 2001 (Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series 1, 2004); page text read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; chapter 7 section 7.1
Energy supplied by maternal fat stores in well-nourished lactating women

FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome 17-24 October 2001 (Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series 1, 2004); page text read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; chapter 7 section 7.1.4, citing Butte and Hopkinson 1998
0.8 kg per month lost at 27.2 MJ/kg gives 21.8 MJ/month, 170 kcal/day. Undernourished women lose about 0.1 kg per month; no MJ/day is given for them.
Recommended extra food energy, exclusive lactation, first 6 months, well-nourished women
FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation, Rome 17-24 October 2001 (Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series 1, 2004); page text read through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF; chapter 7 section 7.2

Printed as 505 kcal/day (2.8 - 0.72). Undernourished women or those who gained too little in pregnancy: +2.8 MJ/day (675 kcal). The second six months depends on milk rate, which the report calls highly variable.
Butte and King 2005; 749 g/day of milk, 2.8 kJ/g, efficiency 0.80

Check: 749 x 2.8 / 0.80 = 2.62 MJ (my arithmetic; milk energy alone 2.10 MJ). Partial breastfeeding at 550 g/day: 1.93 MJ/day. Less 0.72 MJ/day from tissue stores in well-nourished women gives a net 1.9 MJ/day over a non-pregnant, non-lactating woman.
Milk energy output of lactating women, measured, mean of studies
Total energy expenditure plus milk energy averaged 11.74 MJ/day; with 0.72 MJ/day mobilised the requirement is 11.38 MJ/day.
Energy cost of pregnancy and lactation in the mare
NRC Nutrient Requirements of Horses 2007; the secondary page in the URL column refused (HTTP 402) and the book was not opened

Not found in a readable source. A search summary relays, without opening the page, that the 1989 NRC raised digestible energy 11%, 13% and 20% above maintenance in months 9, 10 and 11 of gestation, and that 2007 lactation needs are 'nearly double' mid-pregnancy ones; the 2007 percentages were not confirmed.

tissue_turnover.title: Cell birth and death rates of tissues: turnover, stem-cell pools and age effects for hepatocytes, cardiomyocytes, skeletal muscle, epidermis, gut, bone, red cells and neurons, with plant leaf and fine-root turnover (task 3019, integration gap CG-15)
tissue_turnover.source: Sender and Milo 2021 (PDF read), Bergmann 2009 and 2015, Heinke 2022, Michalopoulos 2007, Spalding 2013, Sorrells 2018, Bhardwaj 2006, Verdijk 2007, Pawlikowski 2015, Eriksen 2010, Clarke 2008, Manolagas 2000, Catlin 2011, Pang 2011, Higgins and Mahadevan 2010, Barker 2007, Alcolea and Jones 2014, Clayton 2007, Gill and Jackson 2000 (PDF read), McCormack 2015, Reich 2004, Chave 2010, Monteiro and Korner 2013, Wright 2004. Most were abstracts or page text read through fetch tools; where a figure comes from a search summary the Note column says so. Rows marked 'my arithmetic' or 'my conversion' are derived from other rows.
rows: Total cell turnover of the human body
Sender and Milo 2021, Nature Medicine 27:45-48 (PDF text read); reference adult, 70 kg, 170 cm; lifespan is time from last division to death; turnover beta = n / tau

Printed as 0.33 +/- 0.02 x 10^12 cells per day (about 4 million per second); Low and High are value -/+ 1 s.e. (my arithmetic). 86% blood cells, almost all of the rest gut cells; erythrocytes, neutrophils and gut epithelium are about 96% of it. Cells of 30 trillion in the body; the whole count turns over in about 80 days.
Total cellular mass turnover of the human body
Sender and Milo 2021, Nature Medicine 27:45-48 (PDF text read); reference adult, 70 kg, 170 cm; lifespan is time from last division to death; turnover beta = n / tau

Printed as 80 +/- 20 g per day (wet mass of cells that die or are shed), about 0.1% of body mass or 0.2% of cellular mass per day; blood about 40% and gut epithelium about 40% of it. Fat and muscle cells are about 75% of cellular mass but only about 5% of the mass turnover. Whole cells only, not protein turnover inside living cells.
Share of cellular mass turnover from fat and muscle cells
Sender and Milo 2021, Nature Medicine 27:45-48 (PDF text read); reference adult, 70 kg, 170 cm; lifespan is time from last division to death; turnover beta = n / tau

Printed as 'around 5%' for adipocytes and muscle cells together, against about 75% of cellular mass. The paper warns that radioisotope-label estimates for muscle 'tend to indicate nuclei turnover rather than whole-cell turnover'; no whole-cell lifespan for skeletal muscle is given.
Share of body cells never replaced (most brain neurons and eye-lens cells)
Sender and Milo 2021, Nature Medicine 27:45-48 (PDF text read); reference adult, 70 kg, 170 cm; lifespan is time from last division to death; turnover beta = n / tau
Printed as about 0.5% of cells, calculated by the authors from two cited sources; the paper says 'complete turnover never happens'.
Lifespan assumed for stem cells in the census
Sender and Milo 2021, Nature Medicine 27:45-48 (PDF text read); reference adult, 70 kg, 170 cm; lifespan is time from last division to death; turnover beta = n / tau
The authors 'assumed a lifespan equal to the age of the reference person' for stem cells (a convention, not a measurement). The paper gives no rate for stem-pool output.
Mean lifespan of circulating red blood cells

Sender and Milo 2021, Nature Medicine 27:45-48 (PDF text read); reference adult, 70 kg, 170 cm; lifespan is time from last division to death; turnover beta = n / tau; average of three models fitted to 2H2O labelling data
Printed as 116 +/- 3 d; Low and High are -/+ 1 s.e. (my arithmetic). Older radioactive-label estimates are said to be biased by toxicity.
Sender and Milo 2021, Nature Medicine 27:45-48 (PDF text read); reference adult, 70 kg, 170 cm; lifespan is time from last division to death; turnover beta = n / tau; 94 +/- 4 pg per cell
Printed as 2.1 +/- 0.1 x 10^11 cells per day, 20 +/- 1 g per day; a check from marrow progenitors (3.1 +/- 0.5 x 10^11 cells) is described but its result is not printed in the text read.
Red blood cell lifespan in children, and in women
Sender and Milo 2021, Nature Medicine 27:45-48 (PDF text read); reference adult, 70 kg, 170 cm; lifespan is time from last division to death; turnover beta = n / tau; children

Printed as 60 to 80 d in children against 120 d in adults; women also have shorter lifespans and pregnancy shortens it more (no number given in the text read). Value is the middle of the range (my arithmetic).
Higgins and Mahadevan 2010, PNAS 107:20587; master-equation model fitted to hospital blood counts; abstract read
Printed as 'removed after about 120 days, triggered by an unknown signal'. The abstract gives no production rate.
Replication interval of human haematopoietic stem cells in vivo
Catlin et al 2011, Blood 117:4460-4466; X-chromosome ratio change with age in women, checked two ways; abstract read

Printed as about once every 40 weeks (range 25 to 50), which is 1.3 divisions per year (my conversion). Models reproduced transplant data and suggest stem-cell numbers rise from birth to adolescence and then level off; no absolute number given.
Haematopoietic stem cell frequency and output with age
Pang et al 2011, PNAS 108:20012-20017; human marrow, young donors 20 to 35 y against healthy donors over 65; flow cytometry and mouse transplants; abstract text relayed by a search summary

No number. Aged stem cells are more frequent among CD34+ cells, less quiescent and myeloid-biased; lymphoid progenitors decline while myeloid progenitors are maintained. So the pool grows with age; the output mix, not the total, changes.
Neutrophil lifespan in blood, and post-mitotic transit time

Sender and Milo 2021, Nature Medicine 27:45-48 (PDF text read); reference adult, 70 kg, 170 cm; lifespan is time from last division to death; turnover beta = n / tau; from half-lives of 13, 16 and 19 h in the 2H2O study of Lahoz-Beneytez et al

Printed as 0.9 +/- 0.1 d in blood and 5.7 +/- 0.1 d post-mitotic transit in marrow; total turnover 6 +/- 1 x 10^10 cells (18 +/- 4 g) per day. Old labels had given half-lives under 7 h and the paper rejects them.

Sender and Milo 2021, Nature Medicine 27:45-48 (PDF text read); reference adult, 70 kg, 170 cm; lifespan is time from last division to death; turnover beta = n / tau; two to three methods weighted by patients from a meta-analysis
Printed as 5.3 +/- 1.7 d; 1.2 +/- 0.2 x 10^11 cells; 2 +/- 1 x 10^10 cells (19 +/- 8 g) per day. Low and High are -/+ 1 s.e. (my arithmetic). The paper's introduction gives '3-5 d for gut epithelia'.
Sender and Milo 2021, Nature Medicine 27:45-48 (PDF text read); reference adult, 70 kg, 170 cm; lifespan is time from last division to death; turnover beta = n / tau
Printed as 3.4 +/- 0.5 d; 5.6 +/- 2 x 10^10 cells; 1.7 +/- 0.6 x 10^10 cells (14 +/- 6 g) per day. Low and High are -/+ 1 s.e. (my arithmetic).
Sender and Milo 2021, Nature Medicine 27:45-48 (PDF text read); reference adult, 70 kg, 170 cm; lifespan is time from last division to death; turnover beta = n / tau
Printed as 13 +/- 9 d; 1.3 +/- 0.9 x 10^9 cells (1.1 +/- 0.7 g) per day. Low and High are -/+ 1 s.e. (my arithmetic).
Intestinal stem cells and their output
Barker et al 2007, Nature 449:1003-1007; mouse small intestine and colon, inducible Cre lineage tracing; abstract read

Lgr5-positive cells at the crypt base generated all epithelial lineages over 60 days. The abstract says the intestinal lining renews faster than any other adult mammalian tissue and that 'four to six' stem cells at the +4 position were the belief before. No cell-cycle time or stem-cell count for humans is in the abstract; the 2014 review (Barker, Nat Rev Mol Cell Biol 15:19-33) abstract gives none either.
Change of intestinal stem-cell output with age
Sender and Milo 2021 (children's gut lifespan from mouse data); Barker 2007
No human number found. The census says children probably have a shorter intestinal lifespan, 'shown for mice', and gives no adult age trend.
Lifespan of epidermal keratinocytes (basal layer to loss of viable cells)

Sender and Milo 2021, Nature Medicine 27:45-48 (PDF text read); reference adult, 70 kg, 170 cm; lifespan is time from last division to death; turnover beta = n / tau; main values from 1970s and 1980s labelling-index studies; the stratum corneum (dead corneocytes) is excluded

Printed as a range of 25 to 38 d, whose average the paper took as the reference; Value is the midpoint (my arithmetic). 1.2 +/- 0.3 x 10^11 nucleated keratinocytes; turnover 3.7 +/- 0.9 x 10^9 cells (3.1 +/- 0.8 g) per day. Psoriasis shortens the lifespan substantially.
Division rate of mouse tail epidermal progenitors, and of slow-cycling stem cells
divisions per week (progenitors); about once per 3 months (slow-cycling)
Alcolea and Jones 2014, Cold Spring Harb Perspect Med 4:a015206 (review, first 100,000 characters read); mouse tail epidermis

The review says mouse tail progenitors 'divide once a week' on average, that the Figure 2 legend gives about once every 3 months for stem cells, and a model uses 10 to 12 weeks for slow-cycling cells. No division rate for human epidermis, and no age trend, is given.
Clayton et al 2007, Nature 446:185-189; mouse tail epidermis, genetic labelling for up to one year; abstract text relayed by a search summary

Clone-size data fit a single progenitor type that divides to give two, one or no cycling daughters in proportions that keep the tissue level; the abstract says stem cells and transit-amplifying cells dividing at different rates cannot give the observed scaling.
